newsitem.title: INDIA: India panel prescribes major government job cuts.
newsitem.headline: India panel prescribes major government job cuts.

text.p: A high-power panel has recommended sweeping reforms in India's mammoth civil service, including cutting more than a million jobs over the next decade, officials said on Friday.
The Fifth Pay Commission report, a copy of which Reuters obtained, also suggested a downsized government with fewer holidays and sharp pay hikes for government employees.
Analysts said the recommendations would have far-reaching implications for a restructuring of the government.

The report called for the abolition of 350,000 vacant posts, constituting nearly a tenth of the current total strength of the federal government. A government spokesman said there were currently 3.7 million federal government workers.
"There is a need for a perspective manpower plan under which there would be downsizing of numbers by 30 percent in a ten-year period," it added.

The commission, which submitted its report to Finance Minister P. Chidambaram on Thursday, estimated the government would need an annual outlay of 88 billion rupees ($2.4 billion) to meet the cost of the higher pay packets.

However, for the coming 1997/98 (April-March) fiscal year, the bill could come down to 73 billion rupees if the government took into account a postponement of some retirement benefits, the report said.
The commission recommended that the lowest-paid government employee should receive a minimum basic monthly salary of 2,440 rupees ($68), against the current 750 rupees.
The most senior civil servant in the Indian hierarchy, the Cabinet Secretary, would earn basic pay of 30,000 rupees ($838), as against a current 9,000 rupees, it said.
The government is not bound to accept the recommendations but traditionally accepts most of them, public finance economist H.L. Bhatia told Reuters.
"But this time they are strong. The allowances, for example, are recommended to be tax free," he said.

The commission called for a six-day week for government employees as against the current five-day week to add 40 working hours for government staff, with the second Saturday of every month treated as a holiday.
"There could be a freeze on further employment of junior staff while a sharp cut-back in intake has been advocated for the executives," the report said.

Bhatia said the implications of the report were far-reaching because state government employees and workers of state-owned companies would demand that the federal government pay packets be treated as precedents.
"The effect is likely to spread. States and public sector undertakings will also follow, naturally," Bhatia said.
He said the state-owned railway network was also likely to follow suit.
State governments will ask for more aid or a greater share of tax revenues from the federal government to meet an expected demand for higher pay packets, Bhatia said.
The commission recommended only three government holidays every year as against 17 at present.

In multi-religious India, the government has traditionally several religious festivals as holidays. The commission recommended that employees should choose individual quotas out of a pool of other holidays.
The commission also recommended part-time employment for women linked to child birth periods.
It also asked for a way out of stifling hierarchies and government clutter.

"The government needs to be reinvented," the commission said. "Employees could be seated in large ergonomically designed halls in furniture of modular design in an aesthetically pleasing environment."
The commission was headed by retired Supreme Court judge S. Rathnavel Pandian.
($1=35.8 rupees)
